content: Coronaviruses are a large family of viruses capable of causing a spectrum of illnesses in humans, ranging from the common cold to severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS). These viruses also infect various animal species. In late 2012, a novel coronavirus, previously unobserved in humans, was identified in a resident of the Middle East. This virus, now known as Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV), has caused over 2,206 laboratory-confirmed cases of human infection as of May 4, 2018. All patients infected with MERS-CoV have had direct or indirect links to the Middle East. However, limited human-to-human transmission has occurred in other countries, primarily among individuals who recently traveled to the Middle East. Most MERS-CoV patients present with respiratory disease, though secondary complications such as acute renal failure, multi-organ failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and disseminated intravascular coagulation have been reported. Some patients also experience gastrointestinal symptoms, including diarrhea. Approximately 36% of infected individuals have died. While the majority of laboratory-confirmed cases have involved individuals with at least one pre-existing medical condition, many patients were previously in good health. Current evidence suggests that MERS-CoV is a zoonotic virus that has entered human populations in the Arabian Peninsula through direct or indirect contact with infected dromedary camels or camel-related products. Studies have shown that MERS-CoV-specific antibodies are widespread in dromedary camel populations in the Middle East and Africa. Animal seroepidemiological surveys indicate that MERS-CoV has been circulating in camels for decades. Human-to-human transmission has been observed to a limited extent, primarily within households. Such failures have occasionally led to large outbreaks, as seen in Saudi Arabia in April-May 2014 and South Korea in May-July 2015. To date, there is no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission. This document provides standardized guidance for public health authorities and investigators to plan and conduct investigations around confirmed and probable cases of MERS-CoV infection. It should be used alongside other detailed guidelines, such as laboratory testing protocols and study methodologies. The document will be updated as new information about MERS-CoV transmission and control becomes available. In countries with secondary transmission linked to imported cases, the guidance for identifying secondary cases and monitoring community transmission remains applicable, albeit on a smaller scale. Early detection of MERS cases has often relied on the vigilance of clinicians rather than established surveillance systems. Therefore, raising awareness among healthcare providers is critical. An effective detection system should include accessible reporting channels for suspect cases and a robust response mechanism. The WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific has published a guide for event-based surveillance, which complements the activities outlined in this document. The document outlines two main categories of activities for managing newly identified cases: (1) active case finding, case description, and enhanced surveillance in affected areas, and (2) specific studies to address critical public health questions related to MERS. The first category aims to detect cases early for timely isolation and management, describe the epidemiology of cases, monitor close contacts, and assess the extent of virus spread. The second category involves targeted studies to answer key questions about MERS transmission, risk factors, and prevention strategies. When initiating an investigation, it is essential to define clear objectives and use a standardized approach. Investigations should also aim to determine the geographic extent of virus transmission, key epidemiological and clinical characteristics of cases, and whether the efficiency of human-to-human transmission has changed. Laboratory confirmation of a MERS-CoV case should trigger a thorough investigation. However, investigations may need to begin before laboratory results are available for suspected cases. Interviews should be conducted systematically by trained health professionals. A multidisciplinary team should be assembled for investigations, including experts in field epidemiology, clinical assessment, laboratory specimen collection, infection prevention and control, and risk communication. Animal health specialists are also critical team members. Clinical data should include signs and symptoms, disease progression, complications, and pre-existing medical conditions. Laboratory data should include specimen types, test results, and the laboratories performing the tests. Symptomatic contacts should be tested for MERS-CoV, and all contacts, especially healthcare workers, should be tested regardless of symptom development. Active case finding should extend beyond close contacts to identify additional cases in the community. Enhanced surveillance should be implemented in affected areas to detect new cases and assess the extent of transmission. Surveillance enhancements may include daily reporting, expanded laboratory testing, and increased testing of SARI cases. Specimen collection should prioritize lower respiratory tract samples, which are more sensitive for detecting the virus. Blood samples for serological testing should also be collected. Molecular diagnostics, particularly PCR, are the primary method for detecting MERS-CoV. Testing should be conducted in experienced laboratories, and specimens should be sent to reference laboratories for confirmation. Serological assays and viral culture are also valuable tools for confirming infection and studying the virus, though viral culture should only be performed in specialized laboratories. In summary, this document provides comprehensive guidance for investigating and managing MERS-CoV cases, with a focus on early detection, containment, and understanding the epidemiology of the virus.
